EFF Atlas of Surveillance (police surveillance technology, searched by department)

notes: Actual revenues and expenditures for fiscal year 2023-24 (ending June 30, 2024), as the county reported them to the State Controller. Not a budget.

Public schools are run by separate school districts, so they are not included. Counties provide social services, public health, jails and courts for everyone in the county, and city-type services in unincorporated areas.
Water, sewer, electric, gas and solid waste utilities count as utilities; airports, ports and transit as infrastructure; public hospitals as health services.
Counties report capital outlay by fund rather than by service, so it counts as infrastructure.

Internal service funds (charges between departments), depreciation and transfers between funds are left out. Enterprise funds' interest is replaced by their principal and interest payments from the debt forms.
Courts, legal services, prosecutors and public defenders, housing, planning and community development count as overhead.
Debt is principal outstanding at year end on bonds, certificates of participation, other long-term debt, construction financing and leases, as reported.
Political money is not scored: California county candidates file campaign reports with their local filing officer, not with the state.
Transparency practices have not been checked yet, so they are not scored.

Red flags: surveillance programs come from the EFF Atlas of Surveillance, a public database of news reports and public records, searched on 2026-10-20. A town or county with none listed may still have programs nobody has reported. Data center deals, corporate tax breaks and license-plate cameras mapped by volunteers have not been checked for California yet. Most records carry no dollar amount, so each documented program costs a quarter of the red-flag points instead of being counted as spending.
